title: "Get started"

> **R or Rust?** The same functions and arguments exist in
> [R](../../r/index.html) (`verb(m, ...)` for Python's `m.verb(...)`) and
> [Rust](../../rust/basemapper_core/index.html).

basemapper renders MapLibre GL basemaps headlessly with a Rust core: no
browser, display server, GPU or GDAL. Vector styles are drawn by a software
port of MapLibre GL JS's renderer, so maps look as they do in MapLibre.
Everything on this page was run when the page was built; the maps are the
output of the code above them.

## Installation

```sh
pip install "basemapper @ git+https://github.com/ar-puuk/basemapper#subdirectory=py-basemapper"
# or: uv add "basemapper @ git+https://github.com/ar-puuk/basemapper#subdirectory=py-basemapper"
```

See the [home page](../index.html) for conda.

## Choose a style

Every function takes a `style`. The simplest is a named basemap, a
[leaflet-providers](https://leaflet-extras.github.io/leaflet-providers/preview/)
name; `list_providers()` lists them, with the API key some need:

```{python}
import basemapper as bm

for p in bm.list_providers()[:12]:
    print(f"{p['name']:<24} vector={p['vector']!s:<5} raster={p['raster']!s:<5} key={p['api_key_env']}")
```

A MapLibre style URL or JSON works too, and so does tile data: a tile URL,
TileJSON, PMTiles archive or ArcGIS service (see
[Your own tiles and services](05-own-data.qmd)).

## A map on its own

`basemap()` creates a view: a centre and MapLibre zoom (or bounds to fit),
and a size in CSS pixels. In a notebook, a view shows the map:

```{python}
m = bm.basemap("OpenFreeMap.Positron", 720, 405, center=(-111.8887, 40.7556), zoom=12.4)
m
```

`repr()` describes it, and the `get_*()` methods read it:

```{python}
print(repr(m))
print(m.get_bounds(lonlat=True))
print(m.get_attribution())
```

`set_view()` and `set_bounds()` change the view. Here it fits North
Carolina's counties (a GeoDataFrame, from
[geodatasets](https://geodatasets.readthedocs.io)):

```{python}
import geopandas as gpd
import geodatasets

nc = gpd.read_file(geodatasets.get_path("geoda.sids"))
bm.basemap("OpenFreeMap.Liberty", 720, 300, bounds=nc)
```

## Raster and vector, PNG and SVG

Basemaps come as raster tiles (images, like OpenStreetMap's) or vector tiles
(geometry styled on the fly, like OpenFreeMap's). Either renders to a PNG
with `render_png()` or an SVG with `render_svg()`. In an SVG, vector layers
are paths and the labels editable text with the style's fonts embedded;
raster tiles are embedded as images.

```{python}
import os, tempfile

slc = (-111.8910, 40.7608)
raster = bm.basemap("OpenStreetMap.Mapnik", 480, 300, center=slc, zoom=11.5)
vector = bm.basemap("OpenFreeMap.Bright", 480, 300, center=slc, zoom=11.5)

out = tempfile.mkdtemp()
for name, m in [("raster", raster), ("vector", vector)]:
    m.render_png(os.path.join(out, f"{name}.png"))
    m.render_svg(os.path.join(out, f"{name}.svg"))

for f in sorted(os.listdir(out)):
    print(f"{f:<12} {os.path.getsize(os.path.join(out, f)) // 1024} KB")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Show the four files written above.
import base64
from IPython.display import HTML

def uri(f):
    mime = "image/svg+xml" if f.endswith(".svg") else "image/png"
    return f"data:{mime};base64," + base64.b64encode(open(os.path.join(out, f), "rb").read()).decode()

HTML(f"""<table class="table" style="table-layout:fixed"><col style="width:7.5em"><col><col><tr><th></th><th>PNG</th><th>SVG</th></tr>
<tr><th>Raster<br><small>OpenStreetMap</small></th><td><img src="{uri('raster.png')}" style="width:100%"></td><td><img src="{uri('raster.svg')}" style="width:100%"></td></tr>
<tr><th>Vector<br><small>OpenFreeMap Bright</small></th><td><img src="{uri('vector.png')}" style="width:100%"></td><td><img src="{uri('vector.svg')}" style="width:100%"></td></tr></table>""")
```

`render_array()` returns the pixels, for your own compositing, and
`get_bounds()` their extent in Web Mercator:

```{python}
a = vector.render_array()
a.shape, a.dtype, vector.get_bounds()
```

`pixel_ratio` makes images larger with the same view and label layout:
`pixel_ratio=2` for a sharp 2x image, `dpi / 96` for print.

## In a plot

`add_basemap()` adds a basemap under a matplotlib axes' content. It renders
when the figure is drawn, for the axes' extent and at the output resolution,
and credits the provider in the corner:

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

nc_3857 = nc.to_crs(3857)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.6))
nc_3857.plot(ax=ax, column="BIR74", cmap="viridis", alpha=0.75, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.3, legend=True)
bm.add_basemap(ax, "OpenFreeMap.Positron", crs=3857)
ax.set_axis_off()
```

`geom_basemap()` does the same in plotnine, with the arguments of R's
`geom_basemap()`:

```{python}
from plotnine import aes, geom_map, ggplot, scale_fill_cmap, theme_void, theme

(
    ggplot(nc)
    + bm.geom_basemap("Esri.WorldGrayCanvas")
    + geom_map(aes(fill="SID74"), alpha=0.7, color="white", size=0.2)
    + scale_fill_cmap("Blues", name="SIDS, 1974")
    + theme_void()
    + theme(figure_size=(8, 3.6))
)
```

[Plots with matplotlib and plotnine](03-plotting.qmd) has more.


## The tile cache

Tiles are cached on disk, so drawing an area again does not download its
tiles again. They are kept for as long as each server allows (a day when it
says nothing), and the cache looks after itself: expired tiles are deleted,
and past 250 MB the least recently used tiles go first.

```{python}
bm.tile_cache()  # where the tiles are kept
```

```{python}
#| eval: false
bm.tile_cache(max_size=500)         # a 500 MB limit
bm.tile_cache("D:/basemap-tiles")   # another folder, for this session
bm.tile_cache(False)                # no cache, for this session
bm.tile_cache(clear=True)           # delete the cached tiles
```

To keep a folder or limit for good, set environment variables before
Python starts, for example in your shell profile (or a project's `.env`,
if you load one):

```sh
export BASEMAPPER_CACHE_DIR=~/basemap-tiles   # Windows: setx BASEMAPPER_CACHE_DIR D:\basemap-tiles
export BASEMAPPER_CACHE_MAX_SIZE=500
```

R reads the same variables, so one folder can serve both languages. Without
them, Python keeps its tiles in the platform's cache folder:
`%LOCALAPPDATA%\basemapper` on Windows, `~/Library/Caches/basemapper` on
macOS and `~/.cache/basemapper` on Linux.
